演奏者坐在短凳上，單手持硬木小槌敲擊懸於調音竹共鳴器上的青銅鍵，以發出約兩個八度: The player sits on a low stool and holds a small hardwood mallet in one hand, striking bronze keys suspended over tuned bamboo resonators to sound about two octaves, usually on ten keys. A beginner first learns the striking positions and the beat, then practises the interlocking melodic parts (kotekan) of the on-beat part (polos) and the off-beat part (sangish). In a gong kebyar line-up the front-row ugal often signals the ensemble with visual movements, so besides striking, clear gestures and dance-like rhythmic movement have to be practised.

烏格主要用於印尼甘美蘭樂團，尤其見於甘美蘭貢克比亞合奏。它常由合奏領導者之一以單: The ugal is used mainly in Indonesian gamelan, especially in gong kebyar ensembles. It is often played by one of the ensemble's leaders with a small mallet in one hand, with dance-like movement; there is usually only one, lower in pitch, and sometimes a second, higher ugal is used. Its role is mostly to carry the central melody of the piece, and sometimes it hands the melody to the jublag and takes over leading the kotekan.
烏格具有明亮而清晰的音色，金屬琴鍵被敲擊時發出璀璨的音響效果。其音質兼具穿透力與: The ugal has a bright, clear timbre; struck, the metal keys give a brilliant sound. It is penetrating and warm at once, and in the gamelan it stands out without losing softness. Its range is about two octaves and its pitch moderate, neither too sharp nor dull. The bamboo resonators let the sound resonate fully, lengthening each note and giving a long-ringing effect. Compared with the gangsa it sounds more cheerful; compared with the gendèr it sounds a little lighter. In the ensemble the ugal's sound is the central melodic line, able both to lead on its own and to blend with the other instruments into a richly layered texture.
烏格是印度尼西亞甘美蘭合奏中的青銅體鳴樂器，屬金屬琴類，通常有十片琴鍵，音域約兩: The ugal is a bronze idiophone of the Indonesian gamelan, in the metallophone class, usually with ten keys and a range of about two octaves, the keys suspended over tuned bamboo resonating tubes. The player strikes with a small hardwood mallet held in one hand, often with dance-like movement. It is used mainly in gong kebyar ensembles, often played by the leader, carrying the main melody, and after handing the melody to the jublag it can lead the interlocking kotekan. An ensemble usually has only one, lower-pitched ugal, and sometimes a second, higher one.
烏格源自印尼爪哇地區，是甘美蘭樂隊中不可或缺的青銅金屬琴樂器。作為甘美蘭音樂傳統: The ugal comes from Java in Indonesia and is an indispensable bronze metallophone of the gamelan. As an important part of the gamelan tradition, its development is closely tied to Javanese court music culture, and its technique and musical role were refined in Central and East Java. The instrument uses suspended bamboo resonators and is played with a small mallet in one hand, evolving a distinctive dance-like lilt. As gamelan spread through Indonesia, the ugal's place as the leading melodic instrument was consolidated, especially at the core of the gong kebyar line-up. Later, as musical exchange spread around the world, the ugal and the gamelan tradition came to be known internationally, and it became an important musical emblem of Indonesian culture.

The source does not state the materials of the frame, the suspension or the other parts, so these are not guessed at.
